nameStory: The 'showy' part of this plant's name comes from its impressive clusters of bright pink-purple flowers that really stand out in late summer. The 'tick-trefoil' part tells a less pleasant story - those segmented seed pods are designed to stick to anything that brushes past, including your socks, pants, and unfortunately, ticks and other creatures looking for a ride!
description: Showy tick-trefoil is a sturdy perennial wildflower that stands 3-6 feet tall in New England's woodlands and prairie edges. It's a member of the legume family, related to peas and beans, with the characteristic three-leaflet leaves and pea-shaped flowers. From July through September, it produces eye-catching clusters of pink to purple flowers that attract butterflies and hummingbirds. After flowering, it develops those infamous segmented seed pods that hitchhike on passing animals and hikers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright pink to purple pea-shaped flowers arranged in dense, elongated clusters at the top of the plant. Each tiny flower has the classic legume shape with an upper 'banner' petal and lower 'keel' - they feel papery when touched and bloom from July to September.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-part leaves (called trifoliate) with oval leaflets that are 2-4 inches long. The leaflets feel smooth on top but may be slightly fuzzy underneath, and they're arranged alternately up the sturdy stem.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive flattened seed pods that break into triangular segments, each covered with tiny hooked hairs that grab onto clothing and fur with remarkable tenacity. The pods feel dry and papery but cling stubbornly when brushed against.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright perennial growing 3-6 feet high with multiple sturdy stems that feel rigid and slightly ridged when rolled between your fingers. Often forms colonies from spreading underground roots.

habitat: Look for showy tick-trefoil along woodland edges, in prairie remnants, and open areas with partial shade throughout New England. It thrives in disturbed areas like roadsides and field margins, preferring well-drained soils. You'll often find it growing alongside other native wildflowers in sunny to partly shaded spots from lowlands to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as reddish stems with small trifoliate leaves unfurling. Plants are just getting established and not particularly noticeable yet.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time from July through September when showy pink-purple flower clusters are in full bloom, attracting butterflies and hummingbirds. This is when the plant truly lives up to its 'showy' name.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and those notorious sticky seed pods mature, ready to hitch rides on anything that passes by. Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Dried brown stems persist with empty seed pod remnants, though most identifying features are gone until spring regrowth begins.

funFact: This innocent-looking wildflower is actually a secret agent in agricultural espionage - scientists have discovered it can harbor bean pod mottle virus and pass it to bean leaf beetles, who then spread it to soybean crops, potentially causing millions of dollars in crop damage across the Midwest!
confusionNotes: With over 10 tick-trefoil species in New England, identification can be tricky! Showy tick-trefoil stands out because it's typically the tallest with the most impressive flower clusters. Memory trick: 'showy' means big and bright - look for the largest, most eye-catching pink flower displays in late summer.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Canadian' tick-trefoil in some regions, this plant is widespread throughout eastern North America, not just Canada. The scientific name 'canadense' often just means 'of northeastern North America' in botanical naming, which can be confusing since many 'canadense' plants grow well south of the Canadian border.
compareHints: Among its tick-trefoil relatives, showy tick-trefoil is typically the tallest and most robust, with the largest and most densely packed flower clusters. Panicled tick-trefoil has more loosely arranged flowers, while round-leaved trailing tick-trefoil stays much lower to the ground. The 'showy' really does live up to its name compared to its more modest cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many ticktrefoils, panicled ticktrefoil stands out with its distinctly narrow, lance-shaped leaflets - much thinner than the broad leaflets of showy tick-trefoil or the rounded leaves of round-leaved trailing tick-trefoil.
Among the tick-trefoils, this is the only one with perfectly round leaflets and a distinctly trailing growth habit.
Among the tick-trefoils, this species stands out for its height and smooth appearance.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, Maryland tick-trefoil is distinguished by its relatively small, smooth leaflets and delicate overall appearance.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, little-leaf stands out for its distinctly smaller leaflets and notably hairy stems.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, perplexed tick-trefoil is most easily confused with tall tick-trefoil, requiring expert examination to separate reliably.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, the toothed variety stands out for its distinctly serrated leaf edges - most other species have smooth or only slightly toothed leaflets.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, hoary tick-trefoil is the gray ghost - its fuzzy, grayish appearance makes it unmistakable.
Among New England's ticktrefoils, sessileleaf is the only one with leaves that attach directly to the stem without stalks - all its relatives have obvious leaf stems.
Among the tick-trefoils, stiff tick-trefoil stands out for its rigid, unbending stems - most others like showy tick-trefoil or panicled tick-trefoil have flexible stems that sway easily.
